title: How Wolves Became Dogs (The Funny History of Man's Best Friend)
blurb: How did a wild wolf turn into the dog on your couch? Campfire scraps, a 14,000-year-old good boy, a Soviet fox experiment, the muscle behind puppy dog eyes, ancient Egyptian dog art and the Victorian breed boom. Four TRUE or FALSE checkpoints along the way, so keep score 👇

beats.say: This is a wolf. Big teeth. Wild. Absolutely will not fetch your slippers.
And this is also, technically, a wolf. Same family tree. Somehow one of them ended up sleeping on your couch and stealing your socks.
So how did a wild wolf turn into a golden retriever? Today, the whole story. And there are four true or false checkpoints along the way, so keep score.
Let's start at the very beginning. Every dog on Earth, from a tiny chihuahua to a giant Great Dane, comes from wolves.
True or false? Dogs come from the same gray wolves that live today.
beats.quiz:
DOGS COME FROM
TODAY'S
GRAY WOLVES
beats.bonus: Dogs and wolves are so closely related that they can still have puppies together.

beats.say: False. Dogs and today's gray wolves are more like cousins. Both come from an older population of wolves that doesn't exist anymore.
So your dog isn't the grandkid of the wolf at the zoo. More like a cousin who moved to the suburbs.
beats.text:
COUSINS.
ONE MOVED TO
THE SUBURBS.

beats.say: And when did this happen? At least fifteen thousand years ago, and maybe a lot earlier. Before farms. Before towns. Before anyone had even invented a leash.
Where it happened is still argued about. Scientists have suggested Europe, Siberia and East Asia. Dogs are very good at keeping secrets.
Wolves are seriously impressive animals. They live in family packs, they work together to hunt, and they can travel huge distances. Basically, a sports team with fur.
So the plan was to take this elite athlete and teach it to sit for a cracker. Bold move, humanity.
So how do you turn a wolf into a friend? One popular idea goes like this. Early humans were hunters, and hunters leave leftovers.
Picture it. A campfire, some bones, and a wolf in the dark going, I'm not saying I'm hungry. I'm just saying I'm here.
The wolves that were a little less scared of people could sneak closer and grab the scraps. The jumpy ones stayed hungry. Over many generations, the calmer wolves did better.
Humans got something too. A wolf nearby barks when something sneaks up in the night. Free alarm system. No batteries required.
Another idea is that people raised wolf pups themselves. The real story may be a bit of both. Either way, it was the best deal in history.
Now, here's one of my favorite clues. In Germany, archaeologists found a grave about fourteen thousand years old. Inside were two people. And a dog.
True or false? People were already taking care of sick dogs fourteen thousand years ago.
beats.quiz:
PEOPLE CARED
FOR SICK DOGS
14,000 YEARS AGO
beats.bonus: Dogs were sometimes buried alongside people in the ancient world, a sign of how much they mattered.

beats.say: True! Scientists found that this puppy had been very sick with a dog disease called distemper.
A puppy that sick could only survive with weeks of care. Keeping it warm, keeping it fed, keeping it clean. And it did survive for a while. Somebody really loved that dog.
Fourteen thousand years ago, someone was already the kind of person who stays up all night with a sick puppy.
And that grave tells us something big. By then, dogs weren't just useful. They were family. People cared enough to bury them like one of their own.
But wait. How did a wolf end up with floppy ears and a curly tail? For that, we need to talk about foxes. Yes, foxes.
In nineteen fifty nine, a scientist in the Soviet Union called Dmitry Belyaev started breeding silver foxes, and he picked only the friendliest ones each generation.
After many generations, the friendly foxes wagged their tails, whined for attention, and wanted to be held. And some of them started to look different, with floppy ears, curly tails and patchy coats.
He chose them for being nice, and he got cuteness as a free bonus. Like ordering fries and getting a milkshake for free.
beats.text:
PICKED FOR NICE.
GOT CUTE
FOR FREE.

beats.say: That's a big hint about dogs too. Choose friendly animals for long enough, and their bodies can change along with their personalities.
Now let's talk about your dog's most powerful weapon. Not the teeth. The eyes.
True or false? Wolves can make puppy dog eyes just as well as dogs can.
beats.quiz:
WOLVES CAN DO
PUPPY DOG EYES
TOO
beats.bonus: Even young puppies can follow a human pointing finger, which is hard even for wolves raised by people.

beats.say: False. In twenty nineteen, scientists found that dogs have a small muscle above the eye that lifts the inner eyebrow. Wolves mostly don't have it.
When a dog lifts that eyebrow, its eyes look bigger and a bit sad, like a baby's. And people respond to that face. We can't help it.
So dogs basically evolved a muscle for getting snacks. Respect.
Dogs also got really good at reading us. They watch our faces, follow where we look, and can tell a happy voice from an angry one. That's not magic. That's thousands of years of practice.
Your dog has been studying you for fifteen thousand years. You've been studying it for about a weekend.
Then, around ten thousand years ago, people started farming. Wheat, barley, bread. And dogs changed their menu too.
Many dogs carry extra copies of a gene for digesting starch, the stuff in bread and grains. Wolves mostly don't. Living next to farmers paid off.
So when your dog stares at your toast, it's not being rude. It's being historically accurate.
Dogs also got jobs. Hunting, herding, guarding. And ancient people loved them so much that they put them in art. This painting comes from an Egyptian tomb more than three thousand years old.
Here's another one. That's a dog sitting under its owner's chair, and the Egyptians even wrote down its name. Ebony. A good name for a good boy.
And this is a little ivory dog from ancient Egypt. Pull a lever, and its mouth opens and closes. A dog toy, for people. Over three thousand years old.
The Romans loved dogs too. Some Roman houses had a mosaic at the door that said cave canem. That means beware of the dog.
Two thousand years later, people still put beware of the dog signs up. Usually for a dog that weighs about eight pounds.
And then there's the nose. A dog's sense of smell is far, far stronger than ours, which is why dogs are used to sniff out everything from lost hikers to bed bugs.
You smell dinner. Your dog smells dinner, who cooked it, what they had for lunch, and a squirrel from Tuesday.
Fast forward to France in the seventeen seventies, where some dogs were living better than most people. This is a real dog bed from that time. Velvet. Gold paint. A tiny palace.
Some say it belonged to Marie Antoinette. Either way, that dog had a nicer bedroom than I do.
And now the big twist. Most of the dog breeds you know are surprisingly new.
True or false? Most dog breeds are less than two hundred years old.
beats.quiz:
MOST DOG BREEDS
ARE UNDER 200
YEARS OLD
beats.bonus: The first organized dog show was held in England in eighteen fifty nine.

beats.say: True! Dogs have helped people for thousands of years, but most of today's breeds were shaped in the eighteen hundreds and after.

In Victorian England, dog shows became a craze. The first organized dog show was held in eighteen fifty nine, and the Kennel Club started in eighteen seventy three. Breeders began writing strict rules for how each breed should look.
These collector cards are from eighteen ninety. Look at this Pomeranian. Fluffier than a cloud, and still, deep down, a wolf.
This is a Mexican Hairless, a breed with a much older history in the Americas. So not every breed is new. Just most of them.
So when someone says their breed is ancient and noble, there's a decent chance it's younger than the light bulb.

Meanwhile, not every wolf story has a happy ending. Japan once had its own small wolves. People carved them, like in this little wooden carving. But by the early nineteen hundreds, the Japanese wolf was gone.
Which is a good reminder. Dogs are everywhere now, but their wild cousins still need looking after.
Not every dog stayed at home, though. Meet the dingo. Dingoes come from early dogs that people brought to Australia thousands of years ago.
Once they got there, they went back to the wild life. No leashes, no baths, no little sweaters. They hunt on their own and live in packs.
Every other dog went from wild to cozy. The dingo went, actually, no thanks.
And today? There are hundreds of millions of dogs on Earth. Herding dogs, rescue dogs, guide dogs, and couch dogs who are very busy doing absolutely nothing.
All of it started with a wolf, a campfire, and a deal. You get scraps, we get a friend. Fifteen thousand years later, it's still the best deal ever made.
And your dog still thinks it's a wolf. It's just a wolf who's scared of the vacuum cleaner.
beats.text:
A WOLF WHO'S
SCARED OF
THE VACUUM

beats.say: So next time your dog does that head tilt, remember. That's thousands of years of wolf history, staring at you, waiting for you to drop a chip.
Scores! The answers were false, true, false and true. How many did you get out of four? Tell me in the comments, along with your dog's name, because I want to know.
And subscribe, because next time we're finding out how cats took over the world. Spoiler. They didn't ask permission.
